transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I’m here because… I’ve started having thoughts that really frightened me. Not like I have some plan, or that I want to do anything, but I keep catching myself thinking it would be easier if I just didn’t wake up. And then sometimes, especially on the drive home after work, my mind goes to this awful place where I wonder if my family, or even my students, would somehow be better off without me.

I know that sounds terrible saying it out loud. I’m a teacher, I’m supposed to be responsible and steady, and I don’t want to act on those thoughts. That’s part of why I came in, because the fact that they’re showing up at all really scares me.
When those thoughts come up, do they feel like unwanted thoughts that pop into your mind against your will?

Yes… I think that’s exactly what scares me. They feel unwanted. It’s not like I sit down and decide to think that way, or like I’m making some kind of plan. It’s more like I’ll be driving home from work, and out of nowhere this thought comes in — like maybe it would be easier if I didn’t wake up, or maybe my family and my students would be better off without me — and then I feel horrified that I even thought it.

I don’t want to act on it. I really don’t. But the fact that it pops into my mind at all makes me feel like something is very wrong, and then I get scared of myself, I guess.
When those thoughts show up, do you find yourself doing anything over and over to make sure you wouldn’t act on them?

I… I don’t think so? Not in a repeated way, at least. I’m trying to think if there’s anything I do like that, because I don’t want to miss something important.

When the thoughts happen, I usually just get really upset and sort of try to push them away, or I’ll sit there feeling guilty and shaken by it. But I don’t think I have a ritual or a specific thing I do over and over to prove I won’t act on them. It’s more like I feel scared that the thought happened at all, and then I keep turning it over in my head afterward, wondering what it says about me.

I mean, I do sometimes reassure myself that I don’t want to do anything, or remind myself of my family and my students, but I’m not sure if that’s what you mean. It doesn’t feel like a repeated checking thing exactly. It feels more like panic and shame after the thought shows up.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most days lately?

I… I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, I know I haven’t been feeling like myself, obviously, or I wouldn’t be here. But “down or depressed most days” — I don’t know if I’ve been calling it that in my own head.

Some days I just feel heavy, I guess, or kind of worn out emotionally. But then I’ll tell myself that everyone gets overwhelmed, especially with work and everything, so I don’t always know where the line is. I’ve been trying not to make too big a deal out of it, and then something happens like these thoughts showing up, and it makes me wonder if I’ve been brushing things off more than I should.

So… maybe? I’m sorry, that’s not a very straightforward answer. I can say I haven’t felt okay lately, but I’m not sure I know exactly how to label it.
Have you been enjoying things less than you usually do?

Yes… I think so. Actually, yes, probably more than I’ve wanted to admit.

I used to have things I really looked forward to, not just big things, but normal parts of my week. Like softball used to be this thing where even if I was tired after school, once I got there and started warming up with everyone, I’d feel lighter. And book club too — I used to actually read the book and have opinions and enjoy the conversation. I have a little garden at home, and normally I’d be out there checking on things, fussing over the plants more than necessary. And the robotics club at school — that used to be one of the parts of teaching that made me feel really energized, seeing the students get excited and problem-solve.

Lately, though, it’s like I’m physically present sometimes, but not really in it. I go through the motions. I show up because I said I would, or because people expect me to, but I’m not getting the same feeling from it. And sometimes I just cancel. I’ll tell myself I’m too tired or that I have grading to do, but if I’m honest, it’s more that none of it sounds enjoyable anymore. Even the things that used to feel like “me” just feel like obligations now.
For the past two weeks, have you felt down, depressed, or hopeless nearly every day?

I’m honestly still not sure how to say that exactly. Nearly every day sounds so definite, and I keep second-guessing myself because I don’t know if what I’ve been feeling “counts” as depressed or hopeless in the way you mean.

I can say I’ve felt not okay a lot of the time these past couple weeks — kind of low, heavy, like I’m dragging myself through things. But I don’t always wake up and think, “I’m depressed.” Sometimes I just think I’m tired, or stressed, or that I need to get through the day and stop overthinking it.

Hopeless… I don’t know. That word feels intense. I don’t know if I’d say hopeless nearly every day. There have been moments where everything feels pointless or like I can’t see myself getting back to normal, but then I’ll also tell myself I’m being dramatic or that it’ll pass.

So I guess the most honest answer is: maybe, but I’m not completely sure. I’ve felt down a lot lately, probably more days than not, but I don’t know if I can confidently say nearly every day.
Did all of this start after a specific stressful event or major change in your life?

I think… yes, there was a specific work thing, though it didn’t feel like a single dramatic event at the time. It was more like a major change in what I was carrying.

It started around when I took over the STEM assessment redesign at school, on top of my regular teaching load. That was about… a year and seven months ago now, I think. I remember thinking I could handle it because it was important, and I cared about doing it well, and I didn’t want to be the person who said no. But it became this constant extra layer on everything I was already doing.

At first I told myself it was just a busy term, or that once we got through the next deadline it would settle. But it never really did. It’s hard to separate what started when, because teaching is always busy, but when I look back, that’s when things started changing for me. That was the point where I stopped feeling like I could quite catch up.
Have you been feeling this way continuously for the past two years?

No, not two years. It feels like a long time, honestly, long enough that it’s hard to remember what I felt like before, but when I actually count it out, it’s been about a year and seven months.

It started around when I took over that STEM assessment redesign at school, on top of my regular teaching. That’s the point I keep coming back to when I try to trace it. I don’t think I was feeling like this continuously before then, at least not in the same way. Since then, though, it’s felt pretty ongoing.
Have there been separate periods in your life before this past year and a half when you felt depressed and lost interest in things for at least two weeks?

I’m not completely sure, honestly. I don’t think there was a clear separate period like that before this, not one that stands out to me as “yes, that was definitely two weeks where I was depressed and lost interest in everything.”

I’ve had stressful patches before, definitely — I mean, I think most people have — and times where I felt low or overwhelmed, especially with work or life stuff. But I don’t know that I’d describe them as the same as what’s been happening this past year and a half. I don’t remember a distinct episode where I stopped enjoying things for at least two weeks in a way that felt obvious at the time.

It’s possible I’m forgetting or minimizing it, because I tend to push through and not label things until much later. But if you’re asking whether there was a clear earlier period like this, I’d say… not that I can really identify.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about a lot of different things?

I’m not sure I’d say “a lot of different things,” exactly. I mean, I do worry, but I don’t know where the line is between normal worrying and excessive worrying, especially when things feel like they actually need worrying about.

A lot of it tends to be… practical, I suppose? Like whether I’ve missed something, whether I’ve let something slip, whether I’m keeping up properly. But I don’t know that I sit there worrying about every area of my life all the time, if that’s what you mean. It’s more like certain things get stuck in my head and I go over them more than I probably need to.

So… I guess yes, I worry, but I’m not sure I’d describe it as excessive worry about lots of different things. I’d maybe need you to clarify what you mean by that.
If that work burden were removed, do you think you’d still feel this way?

I don’t really know. I’ve thought about that a lot, actually, because part of me wants to say yes, of course, if the workload disappeared then I’d feel better. It would be such a relief not to have that constant pressure sitting there.

But I’m not sure it’s that simple. I can’t quite tell anymore what’s caused by the work burden and what’s just… become the way I feel. If it were removed, maybe I’d improve a lot, or maybe I’d still feel flat and worn down because I’ve been in that state for so long. I haven’t had a real chance to test it, if that makes sense.

So I suppose my honest answer is: I’d expect some relief, but I’m not confident I’d suddenly feel like myself again.
When those thoughts come up, do they feel senseless or out of character for you?

They don’t feel senseless, exactly. That’s part of what scares me, I think. In the moment they can feel… almost logical, like my brain is making an argument that everyone would be less burdened if I just wasn’t there. Especially on the drive home, when I’m already exhausted and going over everything I’ve done wrong or might have failed at, I’ll catch myself wondering whether my family or even my students would be better off without me.

But then another part of me is horrified by it, because it doesn’t feel like who I want to be. I don’t want to act on those thoughts. I’m here because I’ve started having thoughts like it would just be easier if I didn’t wake up, and that really frightened me. It feels out of character in the sense that I don’t want to die, not really — I just sometimes want everything to stop, and then I feel ashamed and scared that my mind even goes there.
Over the past two weeks, have you lost interest or pleasure in things nearly every day?

Yes… I think so. Nearly every day, really.

It’s not that I never do anything anymore, exactly, but the feeling has gone out of it. I used to really look forward to things like softball, and book club, and working in my garden. Even the robotics club at school used to be something I genuinely enjoyed — I’d get excited about the students’ ideas and the little breakthroughs they’d have. Now I still sometimes show up, or I tell myself I should show up, but it feels like I’m just sort of… performing the actions of a person who enjoys those things.

A lot of the time I cancel, honestly. I’ll think about book club and instead of feeling pleased to see people or talk about the book, it just feels like another thing I have to get through. With softball, I used to like the routine of it, being outside, being with the team, moving around. Now I’ll make excuses not to go, or if I do go, I’m just waiting for it to be over.

And the garden is maybe the strangest one, because that used to be very calming for me. I used to notice little things — new growth, weeds, what needed pruning — and now I look at it and feel almost nothing. So yes, I’d say I’ve lost interest and pleasure in most of the things I used to enjoy, and it’s been happening pretty much every day.
Have you had trouble sleeping lately?

Yes, definitely. I’m tired all the time, but then when I actually get into bed, my mind just… won’t shut off.

I’ll be physically exhausted, like my body feels heavy and I’m desperate to sleep, but I’ll lie there replaying things from school — assessment deadlines, whether I’ve marked enough, whether I missed something important, some tiny mistake I made in a classroom conversation that probably no one else even noticed. It just loops. I’ll think, okay, stop thinking about it, you need to sleep, and then I’m still lying there half an hour later going over the same thing again.

And then even if I do fall asleep, I’ve been waking up really early, around 4 a.m. a lot of mornings. Not just briefly waking up and rolling over — I mean properly awake, with that awful feeling like the day has already started in my head. I try to get back to sleep, but usually I just sort of lie there, checking the time, calculating how little sleep I’ve had, and then worrying about how I’m going to manage the day. So yes, sleep has been really difficult lately.
If school were out of session and you had no work responsibilities for a week, do you think you would still feel this loss of interest and emotional heaviness?

Yes… I think I would. I mean, school definitely makes it worse, because there’s always something to worry about or prepare for, but it doesn’t feel like this is only work.

If I had a week off, I don’t think I’d suddenly be excited about things again. Softball would still feel like something I should go to rather than something I want to do. Book club would probably still feel like another social obligation, even if I had technically “rested.” And my garden… I know that sounds small, but that used to be something I’d naturally drift toward when I had free time. Now I look at it and it’s like I can see what needs doing, but I don’t feel that little pull to do it.

Even robotics club — which is work-adjacent, I suppose, but it used to feel different from the rest of school — it used to give me energy. Now I mostly just go through the motions, or I cancel things when I can, because none of it really feels enjoyable anymore. So yes, I think even without school for a week, that heaviness and lack of interest would still be there.
Have these symptoms started to interfere noticeably with your ability to do your job or manage things at home?

Yes. I think that’s the part that’s started to really frighten me, honestly, because it’s not just that I feel bad privately and then I can still function normally. It’s showing up in very concrete ways.

At school, I’m falling behind on grading in a way that I don’t usually. I’ve always been the kind of teacher who stays on top of marks and feedback — maybe not perfectly, but reliably. Lately I keep putting it off, or I sit down to do it and I just stare at the stack or the online submissions and it feels impossible to start. Then it piles up, and the students are waiting longer for feedback, and I know that affects the classroom because I’m not as prepared for where they actually are.

Lesson planning has been the same. I’m still getting through the day, but it feels much more like scrambling. I used to have a sense of where a unit was going, what I wanted them to get out of it, what needed adjusting. Now I’m doing more last-minute planning than I’m comfortable admitting. I can get through a lesson, but it doesn’t feel like I’m teaching the way I normally would.

There was also a grading mistake recently that really scared me. Not because it was catastrophic, exactly, but because I used to be so meticulous about that kind of thing. I’d double-check, I’d notice discrepancies, I’d catch myself. And this time I missed something I really should have caught, and when I realized it, I just felt this awful sinking feeling, like… this isn’t me, or at least it didn’t used to be.

At home, I’m managing the absolute basics, but not much beyond that. And socially, I’ve really stopped showing up for people the way I used to. I don’t call family back as quickly, I avoid making plans with friends, I cancel things or let messages sit because even replying feels like another task. So my life has gotten very small. It’s basically get through school somehow, come home exhausted, do the minimum, and then start over.
During this past year and a half, was there ever a stretch of at least two weeks when you felt depressed nearly every day?

Yes. Definitely. It hasn’t really been just a short patch, unfortunately.

I’d say this has been going on for about… a year and seven months now, roughly. It started around the time I took over the STEM assessment redesign on top of my normal teaching load. At first I thought it was just stress from that, like, okay, I’ve taken on too much and I’m overwhelmed, and once I get through the next phase it’ll lift. But it didn’t really lift.

And within that whole period, yes, there have absolutely been stretches of more than two weeks where I felt depressed nearly every day. Honestly, it’s been more continuous than I want to admit. Some days are a little less bad than others, but it’s not like I had a clear two-week break where I felt like myself again.
Around the time this started, did you go through a major loss or upsetting life event outside of work?

Not really… at least, not that I can point to clearly.

I’ve gone over that in my head a lot, because it would almost feel easier if there were one obvious thing I could name — like a death in the family, a breakup, something happening at home — but I don’t think there was anything like that around when it started. Nothing major outside of work that stands out as the beginning of it.

There were ordinary life stresses, I suppose, the kind everyone has, but not some big upsetting event that explains it neatly. That’s part of what has made it confusing for me. It felt like it began around the work pressure increasing, but outside of that, I can’t think of a major loss or life event that set it off.
During this past year and a half, have you ever had a period of at least a few days when you felt like your usual self again?

Not really in a way that felt like a proper stretch, no.

I mean, this has been going on for about a year and seven months now, since I took over the STEM assessment redesign on top of my regular teaching load, and during that time I don’t think I’ve had several days where I thought, “Oh, there I am, I feel like myself again.” There might be a day here or there where I’m functioning a bit better or I’m distracted enough that it feels less heavy, but I wouldn’t describe it as feeling back to normal for a few days in a row.

It’s more like the same thing has just kept running in the background since all of that started.
Have you been having trouble concentrating?

Yes, very much so. That’s actually been one of the more frustrating parts, because my job depends on being able to think clearly and make judgments.

Like, I’ll be marking student work and I’ll read the same response three or four times, and I still won’t know what score to give it. Not because the answer is especially complicated, necessarily — it’s more like my brain won’t hold onto what I just read, or I can’t compare it properly to the criteria. I’ll keep going back to the rubric and then back to the response, and I just sort of… stall.

And even small decisions take me ages now. Something simple like choosing which lab supplies to order can turn into this whole hour-long thing, where I’m going back and forth over options that I normally would’ve handled quickly. It makes me feel inefficient and honestly a bit embarrassed, because these are things I used to just do as part of the day.

doctor.question: When those thoughts come up, do they feel like unwanted thoughts that pop into your mind against your will?

patient.answer:
Yes… I think that’s exactly what scares me. They feel unwanted. It’s not like I sit down and decide to think that way, or like I’m making some kind of plan. It’s more like I’ll be driving home from work, and out of nowhere this thought comes in — like maybe it would be easier if I didn’t wake up, or maybe my family and my students would be better off without me — and then I feel horrified that I even thought it.

I don’t want to act on it. I really don’t. But the fact that it pops into my mind at all makes me feel like something is very wrong, and then I get scared of myself, I guess.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the suicidal thoughts are ego-dystonic obsessions characteristic of OCD by assessing for compulsive reassurance-seeking or mental checking in response to them.
doctor.question: When those thoughts show up, do you find yourself doing anything over and over to make sure you wouldn’t act on them?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically asking about repetitive behaviors or checking rituals to make sure I would not act on the thoughts, which is not covered by the listed symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I… I don’t think so? Not in a repeated way, at least. I’m trying to think if there’s anything I do like that, because I don’t want to miss something important.

When the thoughts happen, I usually just get really upset and sort of try to push them away, or I’ll sit there feeling guilty and shaken by it. But I don’t think I have a ritual or a specific thing I do over and over to prove I won’t act on them. It’s more like I feel scared that the thought happened at all, and then I keep turning it over in my head afterward, wondering what it says about me.

I mean, I do sometimes reassure myself that I don’t want to do anything, or remind myself of my family and my students, but I’m not sure if that’s what you mean. It doesn’t feel like a repeated checking thing exactly. It feels more like panic and shame after the thought shows up.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the unwanted thoughts occur in the context of a broader depressed mood, which would help distinguish a depressive episode from anxiety, adjustment disorder, or OCD-spectrum intrusive thoughts.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling down or depressed most days lately?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depressed mood most days, but the provided symptom profile does not include a specific item for depressed mood.

patient.answer:
I… I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, I know I haven’t been feeling like myself, obviously, or I wouldn’t be here. But “down or depressed most days” — I don’t know if I’ve been calling it that in my own head.

Some days I just feel heavy, I guess, or kind of worn out emotionally. But then I’ll tell myself that everyone gets overwhelmed, especially with work and everything, so I don’t always know where the line is. I’ve been trying not to make too big a deal out of it, and then something happens like these thoughts showing up, and it makes me wonder if I’ve been brushing things off more than I should.

So… maybe? I’m sorry, that’s not a very straightforward answer. I can say I haven’t felt okay lately, but I’m not sure I know exactly how to label it.

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I used to look forward to softball, book club, my garden, and robotics club, but now I mostly go through the motions or cancel because none of it feels enjoyable anymore.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether enjoyment or pleasure in usual activities has decreased, which directly matches loss of interest/anhedonia.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think so. Actually, yes, probably more than I’ve wanted to admit.

I used to have things I really looked forward to, not just big things, but normal parts of my week. Like softball used to be this thing where even if I was tired after school, once I got there and started warming up with everyone, I’d feel lighter. And book club too — I used to actually read the book and have opinions and enjoy the conversation. I have a little garden at home, and normally I’d be out there checking on things, fussing over the plants more than necessary. And the robotics club at school — that used to be one of the parts of teaching that made me feel really energized, seeing the students get excited and problem-solve.

Lately, though, it’s like I’m physically present sometimes, but not really in it. I go through the motions. I show up because I said I would, or because people expect me to, but I’m not getting the same feeling from it. And sometimes I just cancel. I’ll tell myself I’m too tired or that I have grading to do, but if I’m honest, it’s more that none of it sounds enjoyable anymore. Even the things that used to feel like “me” just feel like obligations now.

inference.note: Anhedonia supports a depressive syndrome, increasing suspicion for F32.9/F33.9. Lack of clear compulsions keeps F42.9 possible but less favored; no candidate is fully ruled out yet.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has experienced a sustained major depressive mood state, which best distinguishes depressive disorders from OCD, GAD, or adjustment disorder at this point.
doctor.question: For the past two weeks, have you felt down, depressed, or hopeless nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about depressed mood/hopelessness nearly every day, but the provided symptom profile does not include a distinct item for depressed mood.

patient.answer:
I’m honestly still not sure how to say that exactly. Nearly every day sounds so definite, and I keep second-guessing myself because I don’t know if what I’ve been feeling “counts” as depressed or hopeless in the way you mean.

I can say I’ve felt not okay a lot of the time these past couple weeks — kind of low, heavy, like I’m dragging myself through things. But I don’t always wake up and think, “I’m depressed.” Sometimes I just think I’m tired, or stressed, or that I need to get through the day and stop overthinking it.

Hopeless… I don’t know. That word feels intense. I don’t know if I’d say hopeless nearly every day. There have been moments where everything feels pointless or like I can’t see myself getting back to normal, but then I’ll also tell myself I’m being dramatic or that it’ll pass.

So I guess the most honest answer is: maybe, but I’m not completely sure. I’ve felt down a lot lately, probably more days than not, but I don’t know if I can confidently say nearly every day.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a clear recent stressor triggering the symptoms, which would help distinguish adjustment disorder from a depressive or anxiety disorder.

patient.answer:
I think… yes, there was a specific work thing, though it didn’t feel like a single dramatic event at the time. It was more like a major change in what I was carrying.

It started around when I took over the STEM assessment redesign at school, on top of my regular teaching load. That was about… a year and seven months ago now, I think. I remember thinking I could handle it because it was important, and I cared about doing it well, and I didn’t want to be the person who said no. But it became this constant extra layer on everything I was already doing.

At first I told myself it was just a busy term, or that once we got through the next deadline it would settle. But it never really did. It’s hard to separate what started when, because teaching is always busy, but when I look back, that’s when things started changing for me. That was the point where I stopped feeling like I could quite catch up.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the mood/anhedonia symptoms have persisted for at least two years, which would strongly distinguish adjustment disorder from a depressive disorder and help separate single-episode from recurrent depression.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling this way continuously for the past two years?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about 1 year and 7 months, since I took over the STEM assessment redesign on top of my regular teaching load.

patient.answer:
No, not two years. It feels like a long time, honestly, long enough that it’s hard to remember what I felt like before, but when I actually count it out, it’s been about a year and seven months.

It started around when I took over that STEM assessment redesign at school, on top of my regular teaching. That’s the point I keep coming back to when I try to trace it. I don’t think I was feeling like this continuously before then, at least not in the same way. Since then, though, it’s felt pretty ongoing.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms have occurred in distinct depressive episodes rather than as a stress-linked continuous reaction, helping distinguish major depressive disorder (single vs recurrent) from adjustment disorder or generalized anxiety.
doctor.question: Have there been separate periods in your life before this past year and a half when you felt depressed and lost interest in things for at least two weeks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about prior separate depressive episodes before the current illness, which is not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not completely sure, honestly. I don’t think there was a clear separate period like that before this, not one that stands out to me as “yes, that was definitely two weeks where I was depressed and lost interest in everything.”

I’ve had stressful patches before, definitely — I mean, I think most people have — and times where I felt low or overwhelmed, especially with work or life stuff. But I don’t know that I’d describe them as the same as what’s been happening this past year and a half. I don’t remember a distinct episode where I stopped enjoying things for at least two weeks in a way that felt obvious at the time.

It’s possible I’m forgetting or minimizing it, because I tend to push through and not label things until much later. But if you’re asking whether there was a clear earlier period like this, I’d say… not that I can really identify.

inference.note: Removed F33.9 because the patient does not identify clear prior distinct depressive episodes; this supports a current single episode or stress-related condition rather than recurrent depression. Ongoing symptoms for 1 year 7 months after a work stressor keep F43.2 in consideration, though duration is atypical; intrusive ego-dystonic suicidal thoughts without clear compulsions keep F42.9 on the list, and generalized worry/rumination keeps F41.1 possible.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has excessive, hard-to-control worry across many areas of life, which would help distinguish generalized anxiety disorder from depression or adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: Do you find yourself worrying excessively about a lot of different things?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about excessive worry across many different things, which relates more directly to anxiety/generalized worry than to any listed depressive symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d say “a lot of different things,” exactly. I mean, I do worry, but I don’t know where the line is between normal worrying and excessive worrying, especially when things feel like they actually need worrying about.

A lot of it tends to be… practical, I suppose? Like whether I’ve missed something, whether I’ve let something slip, whether I’m keeping up properly. But I don’t know that I sit there worrying about every area of my life all the time, if that’s what you mean. It’s more like certain things get stuck in my head and I go over them more than I probably need to.

So… I guess yes, I worry, but I’m not sure I’d describe it as excessive worry about lots of different things. I’d maybe need you to clarify what you mean by that.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the symptoms are specifically tied to the identifiable stressor, which would help distinguish adjustment disorder from major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, or OCD.
doctor.question: If that work burden were removed, do you think you’d still feel this way?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether symptoms are attributable to the work burden or would persist without that stressor, which is about situational causation/differential diagnosis rather than any specific symptom item in the provided profile.

patient.answer:
I don’t really know. I’ve thought about that a lot, actually, because part of me wants to say yes, of course, if the workload disappeared then I’d feel better. It would be such a relief not to have that constant pressure sitting there.

But I’m not sure it’s that simple. I can’t quite tell anymore what’s caused by the work burden and what’s just… become the way I feel. If it were removed, maybe I’d improve a lot, or maybe I’d still feel flat and worn down because I’ve been in that state for so long. I haven’t had a real chance to test it, if that makes sense.

So I suppose my honest answer is: I’d expect some relief, but I’m not confident I’d suddenly feel like myself again.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the passive death thoughts are ego-dystonic obsessions rather than depressive suicidal ideation, to better distinguish OCD from depression/adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: When those thoughts come up, do they feel senseless or out of character for you?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because I’ve started catching myself thinking it would be easier if I didn’t wake up, and sometimes on the drive home I wonder whether my family and students would be better off without me, which scares me because I don’t want to act on it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the nature of the patient’s thoughts related to not waking up or whether others would be better off without them, which directly concerns suicidal or death-related thoughts.

patient.answer:
They don’t feel senseless, exactly. That’s part of what scares me, I think. In the moment they can feel… almost logical, like my brain is making an argument that everyone would be less burdened if I just wasn’t there. Especially on the drive home, when I’m already exhausted and going over everything I’ve done wrong or might have failed at, I’ll catch myself wondering whether my family or even my students would be better off without me.

But then another part of me is horrified by it, because it doesn’t feel like who I want to be. I don’t want to act on those thoughts. I’m here because I’ve started having thoughts like it would just be easier if I didn’t wake up, and that really frightened me. It feels out of character in the sense that I don’t want to die, not really — I just sometimes want everything to stop, and then I feel ashamed and scared that my mind even goes there.

inference.note: This turn suggests the thoughts are mood-congruent passive suicidal ideation rather than classic ego-dystonic obsessions, so OCD is less likely and depressive disorders become more likely. Current picture supports a depressive episode with anxious distress vs an adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood, given onset after work stressor but persistence/severity now including anhedonia and passive SI. GAD is less supported because worry is not generalized across many domains.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive symptoms are occurring nearly every day, which would help distinguish a major depressive episode from an adjustment disorder with depressed mood.
doctor.question: Over the past two weeks, have you lost interest or pleasure in things nearly every day?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I used to look forward to softball, book club, my garden, and robotics club, but now I mostly go through the motions or cancel because none of it feels enjoyable anymore.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about loss of interest or pleasure in previously enjoyed activities over the past two weeks.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think so. Nearly every day, really.

It’s not that I never do anything anymore, exactly, but the feeling has gone out of it. I used to really look forward to things like softball, and book club, and working in my garden. Even the robotics club at school used to be something I genuinely enjoyed — I’d get excited about the students’ ideas and the little breakthroughs they’d have. Now I still sometimes show up, or I tell myself I should show up, but it feels like I’m just sort of… performing the actions of a person who enjoys those things.

A lot of the time I cancel, honestly. I’ll think about book club and instead of feeling pleased to see people or talk about the book, it just feels like another thing I have to get through. With softball, I used to like the routine of it, being outside, being with the team, moving around. Now I’ll make excuses not to go, or if I do go, I’m just waiting for it to be over.

And the garden is maybe the strangest one, because that used to be very calming for me. I used to notice little things — new growth, weeds, what needed pruning — and now I look at it and feel almost nothing. So yes, I’d say I’ve lost interest and pleasure in most of the things I used to enjoy, and it’s been happening pretty much every day.

inference.note: This turn strengthens a current major depressive episode: patient now endorses loss of interest/pleasure nearly every day for the past 2 weeks, alongside passive death wishes and guilt/burdensomeness thoughts. However, duration/onset tied to a chronic work stressor still leaves adjustment disorder on the differential, and depressed mood criterion remains somewhat equivocal by self-report, so list is unchanged.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a depressive episode from an adjustment disorder by establishing whether a core neurovegetative symptom of major depression is present.
doctor.question: Have you had trouble sleeping lately?

target_item.name: Sleep_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: I can be exhausted and still lie awake replaying assessment deadlines and classroom mistakes, then wake up around 4 a.m. and never really get back to sleep.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about trouble sleeping, which matches sleep disturbance.

patient.answer:
Yes, definitely. I’m tired all the time, but then when I actually get into bed, my mind just… won’t shut off.

I’ll be physically exhausted, like my body feels heavy and I’m desperate to sleep, but I’ll lie there replaying things from school — assessment deadlines, whether I’ve marked enough, whether I missed something important, some tiny mistake I made in a classroom conversation that probably no one else even noticed. It just loops. I’ll think, okay, stop thinking about it, you need to sleep, and then I’m still lying there half an hour later going over the same thing again.

And then even if I do fall asleep, I’ve been waking up really early, around 4 a.m. a lot of mornings. Not just briefly waking up and rolling over — I mean properly awake, with that awful feeling like the day has already started in my head. I try to get back to sleep, but usually I just sort of lie there, checking the time, calculating how little sleep I’ve had, and then worrying about how I’m going to manage the day. So yes, sleep has been really difficult lately.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the depressive symptoms are tied to the stressor or occur independently, to distinguish major depressive episode from adjustment disorder with depressed mood/mixed anxiety and depressed mood.
doctor.question: If school were out of session and you had no work responsibilities for a week, do you think you would still feel this loss of interest and emotional heaviness?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I used to look forward to softball, book club, my garden, and robotics club, but now I mostly go through the motions or cancel because none of it feels enjoyable anymore.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the loss of interest would persist even without school/work responsibilities, so the most directly relevant symptom is Loss_of_Interest.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think I would. I mean, school definitely makes it worse, because there’s always something to worry about or prepare for, but it doesn’t feel like this is only work.

If I had a week off, I don’t think I’d suddenly be excited about things again. Softball would still feel like something I should go to rather than something I want to do. Book club would probably still feel like another social obligation, even if I had technically “rested.” And my garden… I know that sounds small, but that used to be something I’d naturally drift toward when I had free time. Now I look at it and it’s like I can see what needs doing, but I don’t feel that little pull to do it.

Even robotics club — which is work-adjacent, I suppose, but it used to feel different from the rest of school — it used to give me energy. Now I mostly just go through the motions, or I cancel things when I can, because none of it really feels enjoyable anymore. So yes, I think even without school for a week, that heaviness and lack of interest would still be there.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive symptoms are causing significant impairment, which best distinguishes a major depressive episode from an adjustment disorder here.
doctor.question: Have these symptoms started to interfere noticeably with your ability to do your job or manage things at home?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m falling behind on grading and lesson planning in ways that affect my classroom, and the grading mistake scared me because I used to be meticulous. I’ve also stopped showing up for friends and family the way I used to, so most of my life has narrowed to barely getting through school and then going home exhausted.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the symptoms are noticeably interfering with work and home functioning, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes. I think that’s the part that’s started to really frighten me, honestly, because it’s not just that I feel bad privately and then I can still function normally. It’s showing up in very concrete ways.

At school, I’m falling behind on grading in a way that I don’t usually. I’ve always been the kind of teacher who stays on top of marks and feedback — maybe not perfectly, but reliably. Lately I keep putting it off, or I sit down to do it and I just stare at the stack or the online submissions and it feels impossible to start. Then it piles up, and the students are waiting longer for feedback, and I know that affects the classroom because I’m not as prepared for where they actually are.

Lesson planning has been the same. I’m still getting through the day, but it feels much more like scrambling. I used to have a sense of where a unit was going, what I wanted them to get out of it, what needed adjusting. Now I’m doing more last-minute planning than I’m comfortable admitting. I can get through a lesson, but it doesn’t feel like I’m teaching the way I normally would.

There was also a grading mistake recently that really scared me. Not because it was catastrophic, exactly, but because I used to be so meticulous about that kind of thing. I’d double-check, I’d notice discrepancies, I’d catch myself. And this time I missed something I really should have caught, and when I realized it, I just felt this awful sinking feeling, like… this isn’t me, or at least it didn’t used to be.

At home, I’m managing the absolute basics, but not much beyond that. And socially, I’ve really stopped showing up for people the way I used to. I don’t call family back as quickly, I avoid making plans with friends, I cancel things or let messages sit because even replying feels like another task. So my life has gotten very small. It’s basically get through school somehow, come home exhausted, do the minimum, and then start over.

inference.note: Current turn further supports a depressive syndrome with functional impairment, but the episode duration and full symptom count are still not definitively established from the dialogue, so major depressive episode vs adjustment disorder with depressed/mixed anxiety-depressed mood remain in the differential.

patient.answer:
Yes. Definitely. It hasn’t really been just a short patch, unfortunately.

I’d say this has been going on for about… a year and seven months now, roughly. It started around the time I took over the STEM assessment redesign on top of my normal teaching load. At first I thought it was just stress from that, like, okay, I’ve taken on too much and I’m overwhelmed, and once I get through the next phase it’ll lift. But it didn’t really lift.

And within that whole period, yes, there have absolutely been stretches of more than two weeks where I felt depressed nearly every day. Honestly, it’s been more continuous than I want to admit. Some days are a little less bad than others, but it’s not like I had a clear two-week break where I felt like myself again.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive symptoms are better explained by bereavement-related adjustment versus a depressive episode by clarifying whether there was a major non-work life stressor or loss tied to onset.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a major loss or upsetting life event outside of work as a possible precipitating factor, but the provided symptom profile only notes onset around increased work responsibilities and does not include any outside loss or life event.

patient.answer:
Not really… at least, not that I can point to clearly.

I’ve gone over that in my head a lot, because it would almost feel easier if there were one obvious thing I could name — like a death in the family, a breakup, something happening at home — but I don’t think there was anything like that around when it started. Nothing major outside of work that stands out as the beginning of it.

There were ordinary life stresses, I suppose, the kind everyone has, but not some big upsetting event that explains it neatly. That’s part of what has made it confusing for me. It felt like it began around the work pressure increasing, but outside of that, I can’t think of a major loss or life event that set it off.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive symptoms are pervasive beyond the work-related stressor, helping distinguish major depressive disorder from adjustment disorder with depressed mood or mixed anxiety and depressed mood.
doctor.question: During this past year and a half, have you ever had a period of at least a few days when you felt like your usual self again?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about 1 year and 7 months, since I took over the STEM assessment redesign on top of my regular teaching load.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the time course of symptoms and whether there were periods of feeling back to normal during the past year and a half, which is most directly related to duration.

patient.answer:
Not really in a way that felt like a proper stretch, no.

I mean, this has been going on for about a year and seven months now, since I took over the STEM assessment redesign on top of my regular teaching load, and during that time I don’t think I’ve had several days where I thought, “Oh, there I am, I feel like myself again.” There might be a day here or there where I’m functioning a bit better or I’m distracted enough that it feels less heavy, but I wouldn’t describe it as feeling back to normal for a few days in a row.

It’s more like the same thing has just kept running in the background since all of that started.

inference.note: Sustained depressed mood/anhedonia, insomnia, impaired functioning, and passive death wishes are now clearly established; symptoms persist despite hypothetical relief from work and are not tied to a discrete adjustment reaction, so F43.23/F43.2 are ruled out.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive episode includes impaired concentration/indecisiveness to distinguish moderate from unspecified depressive episode.
doctor.question: Have you been having trouble concentrating?

target_item.name: Diminished_Thinking
target_item.manifestation: I’ll read the same student response three or four times and still not know what score to give it, and simple choices like which lab supplies to order can stall me for an hour.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about trouble concentrating, which matches diminished ability to think or concentrate.

patient.answer:
Yes, very much so. That’s actually been one of the more frustrating parts, because my job depends on being able to think clearly and make judgments.

Like, I’ll be marking student work and I’ll read the same response three or four times, and I still won’t know what score to give it. Not because the answer is especially complicated, necessarily — it’s more like my brain won’t hold onto what I just read, or I can’t compare it properly to the criteria. I’ll keep going back to the rubric and then back to the response, and I just sort of… stall.

And even small decisions take me ages now. Something simple like choosing which lab supplies to order can turn into this whole hour-long thing, where I’m going back and forth over options that I normally would’ve handled quickly. It makes me feel inefficient and honestly a bit embarrassed, because these are things I used to just do as part of the day.

inference.note: Symptoms now clearly meet a depressive episode with at least moderate severity: >2 weeks of depressed mood/anhedonia plus insomnia, impaired concentration, guilt/worthlessness themes, passive death wishes, and functional impairment. Duration is under 2 years, making persistent depressive disorder less likely; symptoms are not better limited to adjustment disorder given persistence and syndrome-level depression extending beyond the stressor context.
